description: We will work on the harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS data
summary:
We developed Fire Calendar MODIS-VIIRS, an interactive web application designed to analyze, visualize and compare historical fire activity using MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations. Our tool leverages the complementary capabilities of these sensors to explore fire hotspot detections dating back to the early 2000s. The resulting time series relies on a harmonization approach that combines the information from both sensors based on the Fire Radiative Power (FRP).

The application allows users to select a geographic area and a period of interest in order to explore the spatial distribution of hotspots, seasonal patterns, and temporal trends. Two interactive graphs help identify seasonal and annual fire detection patterns. Results from the graphs can be exported in CSV format for further analysis.

After further validation, the application developed will provide hotspot information to various stakeholders, such as emergency managers, researchers, and local authorities.
details:
1. Project Overview

Fire Calendar MODIS-VIIRS is an interactive web application designed to analyze, visualize, and compare historical fire activity using MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations available on Google Earth Engine. The project addresses the challenge of long-term hotspot monitoring. We aim to integrate observations from both sensors, at a similar spatial resolution, into a consistent time series. First, we developed a harmonized hotspot calendar that correlates with fire activity. Graphs tailored to the selected region of interest are also displayed, enabling users to identify seasonal patterns and historical trends in the available data.

2. Methodology and Technical Development

We aimed to assess the sensor characteristics and the fire hotspot observations both in the region of interest and across the globe. Our team initially selected Northern Quebec, Canada, as a test region to develop and assess two approaches for integrating MODIS and VIIRS active fire detections. We divided the work into three objectives (D1, D2, and D3).

  • D1 – 1 km Square Grid: First, using Python, we processed MODIS (2000-2025) and VIIRS (2012-2025) observations spanning 2000–2025 to construct a common spatial grid of 1 km × 1 km. Monthly and annual time series were calculated. Different combination of detection were tested to improving consistency between the sensors. For this part, we downloaded the MODIS Terra and Aqua datasets, as well as the VIIRS fire detection dataset, for the Quebec region.
  • D2 – 10 km Hexagonal Grid: Second, we used the combined fire detection dataset from D1 to display temporal trends on a 10 km hexagonal grid. The resulting information was uploaded as an asset to Google Earth Engine to test the functionality a the web application. This experiment allowed us to investigate how detection thresholds and sensor sensitivity influenced the identification of active fires in the Quebec region.
  • D3 – 5 km Square Grid: Third, we combined the MODIS (2000-2026) and VIIRS(2023-2026) datasets, which are freely available on the Google Earth Engine platform, to create the web application. Both datasets were harmonized by combining the data based on Fire Radiative Power (FRP) and the detection confidence of each product. The datasets were reprojected onto a common 5 km × 5 km grid, a cell size chosen as a compromise to limit the computing time required to display the maps in the application. We also developed code to explore monthly and annual trends in hotspot detection using interactive graphs.

Our final web application used a 5 km × 5 km square grid to explore fire activity worldwide. Together, these steps demonstrated how we used local data points to upscale to a harmonized collection.

3. Data sources and technologies used

We used satellite active fire detection products available through NASA FIRMS and Google Earth Engine, including:

  • MODIS MYD14A1 Version 6.1, providing active fire observations at approximately 1 km spatial resolution in Google Earth Engine (D3).
  • NOAA-20 (JPSS-1) VIIRS Active Fire Detection Product, providing active fire observations at approximately 375 m spatial resolution in Google Earth Engine (D3).
  • MODIS Collection 6.1: Temporal Coverage: 1 November 2000 – present, which is a shapefile providing fire points detected by MODIS sensor (D1 and D2).
  • VIIRS S-NPP 375m: Temporal Coverage: 20 January 2012 - 2 November 2026 which is a shapefile providing fire points detected by VIRS sensor (D1 and D2).

Python was used for processing locally downloaded fire-detection dataset, spatial aggregation, time-series construction, and statistical calibration experiments.

Google Earth Engine (GEE) was used to access open satellite datasets, analyze detection characteristics, perform spatial harmonization, and develop the interactive web application.

The application integrates maps and charts of monthly and yearly fire detection calendar. Users can select a geographic region and period of interest, examine the spatial distribution of hotspots, compare monthly and annual fire detection and export results in CSV format.

4. Innovation and Creativity

The main innovation of Fire Calendar MODIS-VIIRS lies in its experimental approach to integrating satellite fire observations across different spatial scales. The workflow we developed allows us to assess fire activity locally and then upscale this process to the entire globe. The combination of MODIS and VIIRS products from the collections available in Google Earth Engine relies on the harmonization of Fire Radiative Power (FRP). The application brings these satellite datasets together in an accessible visual calendar, making long-term fire activity easier to interpret

5. Benefits and Expected Impact

The application requires further validation. Once validated, the final version of Fire Calendar MODIS-VIIRS is intended for anyone interested in fire activity around the globe. Emergency managers, researchers, and environmental organizations are among the users who could benefit from it. By providing access to past hotspot activity, the application helps users identify fire seasons and detect local hotspot activity patterns. Because it is built on data available in Google Earth Engine, its near-global coverage creates opportunities to monitor fire regimes in remote or data-limited regions. Ultimately, our project aims to make satellite-based fire information more accessible.

6. Technical Challenges and Scientific Considerations

Throughout development, our team weighed several technical and scientific considerations, including differences in MODIS and VIIRS spatial resolutions, sensor sensitivities, and detection confidence levels. To address these constraints, we used Fire Radiative Power (FRP) measurements to harmonize the data into a global dataset. Preliminary steps allowed us to address the complexity of the datasets, to choose the best way to harmonize the data, and to provide validation data. We also considered the trade-off between spatial detail and the computing limitations of the application by choosing spatial resolutions ranging from 1 km to 5 km. To meet the need for a harmonized calendar, we created annual and monthly graphs, and users can easily download the underlying data afterward. Uncertainties related to satellite observation conditions, acquisition frequency, and differences between sensors would require further validation.
